title: Shloka 180
subtitle: The last two seals, three triangles, and one plain word for mother

namas.translation: She is the yonimudrā, the gesture that shapes with the fingers the source from which everything issues.

compound.gloss: the seal that takes the shape of the yoni

children.gloss: seal, ritual gesture of the hands

namas.translation: She commands the trikhaṇḍā, the seal in three sections with which the worship is closed.

compound.gloss: sovereign of the seal made of three parts

namas.translation: Sattva, rajas and tamas are hers to hold, although a few names earlier she was declared free of them.

compound.gloss: she who possesses the three constituent qualities

namas.translation: She is simply Mother, the oldest and plainest term of address a worshipper has.
She occupies the innermost triangle of the Śrīcakra, the enclosure immediately around the point.

compound.gloss: she who resides in the triangle

children.gloss: that which has three corners, a triangle

namas.translation: No fault attaches to her, and none is left in those she takes up.

compound.gloss: she in whom there is no evil

namas.translation: The record of what she has done exceeds anything ordinary causes could produce.

children.gloss: conduct, course of action, way of proceeding

namas.translation: What is genuinely wanted she supplies.

compound.gloss: she who grants the objects desired

commentary.meaning: Eight names, more than any other verse in this closing stretch, and the first line is four of them at four syllables each. It opens by finishing the list the previous verse began: the seal of the source and the mistress of the seal made in three parts are the last two of the ten. Then the same shape keeps recurring in a different register — she holds the three strands of nature, she is Mother, she dwells in the innermost triangle of the diagram. A triangle drawn with the fingers, a triangle drawn on metal, and the threefold structure of the world itself are named within twelve syllables of one another. The second line changes key: no fault attaches to her, what she has done exceeds anything ordinary causes would produce, and she gives what is actually wanted. Two of the eight names are hidden inside sandhi, which makes this verse the best place in the hymn to see how the count of a thousand is arrived at.
commentary.history:
Two names in this verse are invisible unless you know they are there. Triguṇāmbā is triguṇā followed by ambā, the final ā of the first swallowing the initial a of the second; anaghā'dbhutacāritrā is anaghā followed by adbhutacāritrā, and there the avagraha marks the elided vowel. This matters more than an orthographic curiosity should, because the hymn claims a specific number. A thousand names is not a round figure loosely applied; it is an assertion, and the arithmetic only comes out if particular compounds are divided at particular joints. What fixes the divisions in practice is not the running verse text but the nāmāvalī, the list in which every name is put into the dative and followed by namaḥ for use in offering. That list is what a lineage transmits, and it is where the tradition records its decisions about where one name ends and the next begins. Editions and lineages do not agree at every point, and a reader who finds a printed count that differs by one or two from another printing has usually found a place like this one rather than a mistake.

Yonimudrā and trikhaṇḍeśī complete the sequence of ten seals that the previous verse began. The yoni seal is made by interlacing the fingers so that they enclose a triangular opening, and the name of the gesture is the ordinary Sanskrit word for womb, source, or place of origin — the same word used for the socket a thing sits in and for the birth a being takes. The trikhaṇḍā, the seal in three sections, is the last of the set and is shown at the close of the worship. Calling her its īśī, its mistress, rather than calling her the seal itself, is a small piece of care: the gesture belongs to her, as the mantra and the diagram were said much earlier in the hymn to belong to her, and is not the practitioner's property.

Guṇa means a thread or a strand, and the oldest image behind the Sāṃkhya doctrine is a rope of three strands: sattva, clarity, rajas, movement and passion, and tamas, weight and darkness. Everything that is made is made of them in some proportion. To call her triguṇā is to say the rope is hers. This sits against statements elsewhere in the hymn that deny the three strands of her altogether, and the contradiction is not a slip. A hymn of a thousand names is not building a consistent system; it is saying the true things that can be said, including the ones that cancel each other, and the tradition's readers have generally taken the pair to mean that she is not constituted by the strands but is not excluded from them either.

Between triguṇā and trikoṇagā stands ambā, and it is worth stopping on how unlike its neighbours it is. Every other name in this verse is a compound requiring analysis. Ambā is two syllables and is what a child says. The hymn puts it in the middle of its most technical line, and it will end the thousand with the same word in its affectionate form.

Trikoṇagā places her in the innermost triangle of the Śrīcakra, the enclosure immediately surrounding the central point. The diagram is built of nine interlocking triangles, and the small triangle at the heart of it is the last enclosure before the bindu; to say she goes or abides there is to locate her at the end of the inward journey the worship makes.

Of the second line, adbhutacāritrā is the name that opens onto the rest of the literature. Cāritra is conduct or course of action, and what it points to is a story: the long narrative in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa in which this hymn is embedded, where Lalitā arises from the fire-pit of consciousness and destroys the demon Bhaṇḍāsura with her armies and her chariot. The second name of the thousand, near the very beginning, already referred to that birth. Here, six names from the end, the hymn stands back and calls the whole account wonderful — adbhuta, the word used of what cannot be accounted for by ordinary causes.

Vāñchitārthapradāyinī, the last name of the verse, is the first clear sounding of a note that will dominate what follows the thousand names in the purāṇa. But notice what it does and does not say. It is a statement about her, in the nominative, like every other name: she is one who gives what is desired. It is not yet a statement about what reciting the hymn earns. That claim comes later, in the section of promises that follows the stotra proper, and keeping the two apart is worth the effort.
commentary.practice:
The first line is four names, four syllables each, and three of them begin with tri. This is the most easily garbled line in the closing verses, and the remedy is to know why the four are in this order rather than to rely on the sound: two hand-seals first, finishing the list from the previous verse, then the three strands, then the mother, then the triangle she sits in. Fix that sequence and the line will not shuffle.

The retroflexes are the technical work here. Trikhaṇḍeśī has ṇḍ, both made with the tongue curled back, preceded by kha, a single aspirated guttural and not k followed by h. Trikoṇagā has a retroflex ṇ, and triguṇā has another; in both, the retroflexion is caused by the r earlier in the word, which is the same rule that governs tarpaṇa and svarūpiṇī in the two preceding verses. Once you have heard it three times in three verses it stops being a rule and becomes a habit.

In the second line, anaghā has gh as one aspirated sound, and the join with the following name gives you dbhu, a voiced dental stop running straight into an aspirated labial: a-na-ghā-dbhu-ta. The temptation is to insert a vowel. Do not. Vāñchitārthapradāyinī opens with the long ā and then ñch, the palatal nasal against the aspirated palatal ch, which English does not have and which will come out as a plain ch unless you make the nasal deliberately.

Both quarters of the second line are single names of eight syllables, so there is nowhere to breathe inside them; the only pause is at the caesura after the first line's fourth name and at the end. Reciters who run short of air here have usually spent it on the four short names above.

For archanā the eight datives are yonimudrāyai, trikhaṇḍeśyai, triguṇāyai, ambāyai, trikoṇagāyai, anaghāyai, adbhutacāritrāyai, vāñchitārthapradāyinyai. Saying them in this form is the quickest way to convince yourself that triguṇāmbā really is two names, because the two words separate cleanly and each takes its own ending, and the same is true of the pair in the second line. If you have only ever chanted the continuous text, do the eight once in the dative and the shape of the verse will change permanently.

What the verse asks is mostly attention. It is dense with technical vocabulary — two gestures, a doctrine of nature, a region of a diagram — and then it puts ambā in the middle of that and vāñchitārthapradāyinī at the end of it, which are the two most ordinary things a person could say to a goddess: you are my mother, and you give me what I want. The hymn does not treat the technical and the childlike as belonging to different levels of practice. They are in the same four lines, in the same metre, and are offered with the same syllable of homage.

crossReferences.deva: भवानि त्वं दासे मयि वितर दृष्टिं सकरुणामिति स्तोतुं वाञ्छन्कथयति भवानि त्वमिति यः । तदैव त्वं तस्मै दिशसि निजसायुज्यपदवीं मुकुन्दब्रह्मेन्द्रस्फुटमकुटनीराजितपदाम् ॥
crossReferences.iast: bhavāni tvaṃ dāse mayi vitara dṛṣṭiṃ sakaruṇām iti stotuṃ vāñchan kathayati bhavāni tvam iti yaḥ | tadaiva tvaṃ tasmai diśasi nijasāyujyapadavīṃ mukundabrahmendrasphuṭamakuṭanīrājitapadām ||
crossReferences.translation: Wishing to say "Bhavānī, cast on me, your servant, a look that has pity in it," a man gets no further than the two words bhavāni tvam — and at that moment you give him the state of union with yourself, whose feet are waved over by the bright crowns of Viṣṇu, Brahmā and Indra.
crossReferences.relevance: The most exact commentary in the literature on vāñchitārthapradāyinī, and the reason the name should not be read as a vending machine. The poem turns on the fact that the two words the man managed to say can also be construed as "may I become you": he asked for a glance and was given identity, because what he actually wanted was not what he had thought to ask for. The verb the poem uses for his wanting, vāñchan, is the same root as the vāñchita of the name.

crossReferences.deva: सत्त्वं रजस्तम इति गुणाः प्रकृतिसम्भवाः । निबध्नन्ति महाबाहो देहे देहिनमव्ययम् ॥
crossReferences.iast: sattvaṃ rajas tama iti guṇāḥ prakṛtisambhavāḥ | nibadhnanti mahābāho dehe dehinam avyayam ||
crossReferences.translation: Clarity, passion and darkness — these are the strands born of nature, and they bind the imperishable dweller, great-armed one, within the body.
crossReferences.relevance: What the Gītā says about the three strands is that they tie, and everything that has a body is tied by them. Setting that beside triguṇā shows the force of the name: she possesses what binds everyone else, which is a very different claim from being made of it, and it explains why the hymn can also say elsewhere that the strands are not hers at all.

references.title: The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, translated and annotated
references.author: tr. G. V. Tagare, Ancient Indian Tradition and Mythology series (Motilal Banarsidass)
references.note: The complete English of the purāṇa in which this hymn sits, including the Lalitopākhyāna — the account of her arising and of the war with Bhaṇḍāsura. If adbhutacāritrā is to mean anything concrete to you, this is where the deeds are. The translation is serviceable rather than elegant, and the notes are thin, but nothing else in English gives you the whole narrative.

references.title: Yantra: The Tantric Symbol of Cosmic Unity
references.author: Madhu Khanna (Thames & Hudson, 1979)
references.note: Still the best illustrated introduction to how these diagrams are constructed and read. Its treatment of the Śrīcakra shows plainly what trikoṇagā refers to: the small triangle at the heart of the figure, the last enclosure before the point, drawn where the nine larger triangles converge.

references.title: The Saundaryalaharī, or Flood of Beauty
references.author: ed. and tr. W. Norman Brown (Harvard Oriental Series 43, 1958)
references.note: A scholar's edition of the poem, with the Sanskrit, a plain translation, and notes that explain the puns rather than admiring them. Brown's handling of verse 22 in particular sets out the double reading of bhavāni tvam clearly enough that you can see the joke and the theology at the same time.

references.title: Classical Sāṃkhya: An Interpretation of Its History and Meaning
references.author: Gerald James Larson (Motilal Banarsidass)
references.note: For the three strands, which this verse assumes its reader already understands. Larson is careful about what the guṇas are in the classical system — constituents of nature, not qualities of things — and that distinction is what makes triguṇā a strong claim rather than a decorative one.
